title: Google Cloud India Disruption After STT GDC Delhi Data-Center Fire
operator: Google Cloud (impacted tenant); STT GDC / Tata Communications JV (named as the third-party facility operator only by third-party reporting; not confirmed by Google)
text: At the network-engineering level, the incident is a POP-isolation event that exposed a metro capacity-headroom deficit. The Delhi POP was a non-compute node, meaning it hosted networking functions (backbone termination, Internet Edge peering, load-balancing ingress) rather than customer VMs or storage; its emergency de-energization therefore had no data-plane compute blast radius but a large control/transport-plane one. When the POP dropped, the traffic it normally sourced and sinked, particularly peering with large Indian ISPs, had to reconverge onto remaining paths. The observed symptom triad (elevated latency, intermittent packet loss, non-optimal routing) is the classic signature of links driven past their congestion knee: queueing delay rises (latency), buffers overflow (packet loss), and BGP/traffic-engineering shifts push flows onto longer or transit-heavy paths (non-optimal routing). That the three affected products were Hybrid Connectivity, VPC and Media CDN is consistent with an edge/transport failure: Hybrid Connectivity (Interconnect/VPN attachment points) and Media CDN (edge cache egress/peering) are peering- and edge-sensitive, and VPC traffic transiting the metro inherited the degraded paths, whereas core compute regions kept running. The remediation sequence is diagnostic of the root design gap. Google did not simply reroute; it (a) optimized backbone capacity to reclaim headroom, (b) restored then augmented Internet Edge peering, and (c) added capacity on Delhi-Mumbai and Delhi-Chennai backbone links plus out-of-region Chennai peering for redundancy and load-balancing. This is remediation by capacity addition, which only helps if the pre-incident state lacked N-node failover margin, implying the Delhi metro's peering/backbone was single-homed or thin-provisioned through the lost POP. Full restoration further required physical re-entry (~22-23 June) to bring the site's own equipment back, confirming that some capacity was irreplaceable off-site and that fire-safety clearance, not routing convergence, set the recovery clock. What remains unverified and load-bearing for a complete RCA: the ignition source and equipment type (Google never states them; the lithium/UPS/BESS attribution is third-party), and the capacity-planning design (edge N/N+1 tier, single-homing, provisioned failover margin) that Google discloses only as 'reduced available network capacity.' No quantitative impact (error rate, latency-ms, packet-loss %, affected-project count, SLA credit) was published, so severity is characterized qualitatively.

Google states the effect (reduced available capacity) but not the design flaw (single-homing, edge redundancy tier, or provisioned margin), so the deeper cascade cause is inferred, not disclosed.

title: SK C&C Pangyo Data Center Fire and the National Kakao/Naver Outage
text: On 15 October 2022, a lithium-ion UPS battery on the third basement level (B3) of the SK C&C Pangyo Data Center ignited and spread, forcing firefighters and operators to cut power to the entire facility. Because tenant Kakao had concentrated core functions — including its sole authentication service — at this single site, the power cut cascaded into a nationwide outage of KakaoTalk, Daum, Kakao-linked banking, KakaoT and dozens of downstream services. Co-tenant Naver, which kept its own separate data center, was far less affected. KakaoTalk stayed down for more than 11 hours, the longest in its history, and full restoration of all Kakao services took roughly five days. The event triggered a CEO resignation, a three-way blame dispute, and South Korea's "Kakao Outage Prevention Act" mandating geographic redundancy for major platforms.

title: SK C&C Pangyo Data Center Fire and the National Kakao/Naver Outage
text: The immediate cause was ignition of lithium-ion batteries in a UPS system in the B3 battery room, which spread through the building (fuel and location multiply corroborated by Kakao's CEO and police reports; exact thermal-runaway trigger and legal fault remain officially disputed, with SK Group denying responsibility on the basis of its battery-management-system records). The catastrophic recovery, per South Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT, stemmed from a design and architecture failure: the lithium-ion batteries were not physically separated from the UPS, so they resisted the gas fire-suppression system, continued heating the UPS, and forced a full facility power cut-off. This was compounded by Kakao concentrating core functions — including its single authentication/verification service — at one data center with no geographic redundancy.

title: SK C&C Pangyo Data Center Fire and the National Kakao/Naver Outage
text: The engineering crux is the interaction between lithium-ion energy storage and the facility's fire-suppression and power topology. Lithium-ion cells in thermal runaway are self-sustaining exothermic reactions that generate their own oxidizer and are not extinguished by inert-gas (clean-agent) suppression, which is designed to interrupt combustion by displacing oxygen or absorbing heat in ordinary fires. Because the UPS batteries at Pangyo were co-located with — not physically separated from — the UPS itself, the runaway continued to heat the UPS even after gas discharge, meaning suppression bought no time and containment was impossible without removing the energy source. With a spreading fire in an energized electrical room, de-energizing the facility became the only safe action, and cutting power to a UPS-backed data center means the batteries that would normally ride through a utility loss are themselves the hazard being isolated — so there is no bridging power and the load drops instantly. The downstream failure was then a software-architecture problem: with roughly 32,000 servers dark and Kakao's authentication/verification function resident only at this site, every service that gated on login failed simultaneously and could not be failed over — whereas co-tenant Naver, holding a second data center, rode out the same event with only partial disruption. Recovery was bounded by two serial constraints — first, the fire had to be safe enough to restore power (repeatedly deferred for safety on Oct 15), and second, servers and stateful services had to be rebuilt and re-synchronized in stages, a process that itself reintroduced instability (the Oct 16 10:15 photo/video regression) because dependent services were brought up against not-yet-consistent infrastructure. The durable engineering lessons are therefore threefold: isolate and li-ion-rate battery-room suppression and separate it from the UPS; never make a mandatory dependency (authentication) single-homed; and design DR runbooks around the realistic worst case of an instantaneous, multi-day total facility loss rather than component-level degradation.

title: SK C&C Pangyo Data Center Fire and the National Kakao/Naver Outage
text: Failure mechanism: The incident began as a battery-room fire: lithium-ion cells in a UPS system on the B3 basement level entered thermal runaway and ignited, then spread through the building. Critically, the batteries were not physically isolated from the UPS, so the facility's gas fire-suppression system could not extinguish the reaction — the cells kept generating heat and re-feeding the fire. With suppression defeated and a spreading blaze in a live electrical room, the only safe option was to cut power to the entire facility, converting a localized fire into a complete loss of the data center.

title: SK C&C Pangyo Data Center Fire and the National Kakao/Naver Outage
text: Why it cascaded nationally: The blast radius was set not by the fire but by architecture. Kakao had concentrated core functions at this single Pangyo site, including its sole authentication/verification service. When the site went dark there was no geographic failover, so nearly every dependent Kakao service — KakaoTalk, Daum, KakaoT, Kakao Pay, and many Kakao-auth-dependent banking and payment functions — was disrupted at once, and downstream sectors that had built on Kakao (banking, ride-hailing, deliveries, grocery) were hit with them. Co-tenant Naver, by contrast, kept most of its services running by failing over to its own separate data center — the same fire, opposite outcome, determined almost entirely by redundancy. A facility incident thus became a de-facto national-infrastructure outage affecting most of the population.

title: SK C&C Pangyo Data Center Fire and the National Kakao/Naver Outage
text: Recovery dynamics: Recovery was slow and non-linear. Power could not be safely restored quickly, so Kakao's early '2-hour' estimate slipped through a sequence of delay announcements on Oct 15. Restoration proceeded in stages: partial Daum News by 23:21, first KakaoTalk text by 02:16 Oct 16 (~11 hours in), then a server bring-up from 12,000 to 27,000 of 32,000 servers across Oct 16. The staged bring-up on partially recovered infrastructure produced fresh instability — photo/video transmission failed again at 10:15 — and long-tail services (Brunch, Kakao Map, securities/real-estate) trickled back over the following days, with full restoration declared only at 23:00 on Oct 20, a total of 5 days 7.5 hours (~127.5 h).

title: SK C&C Pangyo Data Center Fire and the National Kakao/Naver Outage
text: Organizational and systemic factors: The ICT ministry assigned blame across all three stakeholders. SK C&C was faulted for a sketchy fire-response protocol with no action plans or drills, weak battery monitoring and fire detection, and poor information-sharing with firefighters. Kakao was faulted for concentrating core functions at one site. The accountability fallout included a CEO-level resignation at Kakao and multiple lawsuits, plus a public blame dispute: SK Group — whose subsidiary SK On supplied the batteries and whose affiliate SK C&C operated the facility — denied responsibility, citing its battery-management-system records. The regulatory response was forceful — one-month deadlines for emergency-response plans, ordered fire drills, and a national push toward resilient-services guidelines and the Kakao Outage Prevention Act mandating geographic redundancy.

title: SK C&C Pangyo Data Center Fire and the National Kakao/Naver Outage
text: Cross-incident pattern: This incident sits squarely in a recurring class of failures where a physical-plant event (fire, power) exposes a latent architectural single point of failure. The technical trigger — lithium-ion energy storage that resists conventional suppression and forces a full power cut — is a known and rising risk as li-ion displaces VRLA in data-center UPS fleets. The amplification pattern — one facility, one authentication dependency, no geographic failover — mirrors other national-scale platform outages where concentration, not the initial fault, determined severity, and the sharply better outcome for redundancy-holding Naver in the very same building makes the point concrete. The regulatory outcome (mandated redundancy) reflects a broader trend of treating dominant consumer platforms as critical infrastructure subject to resilience law.

title: NIRS Daejeon Government Data Center: UPS Lithium-Ion Battery Fire During Relocation Work
text: On the evening of 26 September 2025, a lithium-ion UPS battery that had been disconnected in order to be relocated to the basement of the NIRS Daejeon government data center entered thermal runaway and exploded in a server room, igniting a fire that took roughly ten hours to extinguish. When the fire broke out, all 647 government IT systems at the Daejeon headquarters were taken offline (96 of them directly destroyed, the rest shut down as a precautionary safety measure). Core national services including digital IDs, Korea Post postal banking, emergency GPS tracking, courts and tax were paralyzed, and all documents on the G-Drive cloud used by up to 30 ministries and nearly 191,000 employees were permanently lost because the repository was not backed up externally. Recovery reached 70.5 percent by 24 October and later exceeded 95 percent; the NIRS chief and three other officials were booked for causing the fire through on-duty negligence, the chief was relieved of duty, and Daejeon police raided NIRS.

title: NIRS Daejeon Government Data Center: UPS Lithium-Ion Battery Fire During Relocation Work
text: The ignition source was an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) lithium-ion battery that had been disconnected in order to be relocated to the basement of the facility. The battery entered thermal runaway and exploded inside a server room, igniting the fire. Two independent primary reports confirm the causal chain: relocation work on a disconnected lithium-ion UPS battery, which underwent a thermal-runaway explosion that started the server-room fire. Officials were booked for causing the fire through on-duty negligence, framing the legal theory as negligent (not intentional) causation tied to the battery-move work.

title: NIRS Daejeon Government Data Center: UPS Lithium-Ion Battery Fire During Relocation Work
text: The proximate technical event was a thermal-runaway explosion of a lithium-ion UPS battery pack that had been disconnected for relocation to the basement, occurring inside a live server room. Lithium-ion thermal runaway is a self-sustaining exothermic process: once a cell is driven into runaway (by mechanical, thermal or electrical abuse — all plausible during a physical battery move), internal temperatures climb rapidly, the cell vents flammable electrolyte and gases, and heat propagates cell-to-cell through the pack, producing an energetic fire that is difficult to arrest and prone to sustained burning. That the pack exploded in the server room rather than an isolated battery area is the pivotal engineering failure: it placed the ignition energy directly among IT hardware, which is why 96 of 647 systems were physically destroyed rather than merely de-energized. The response profile — 101 firefighters, 31 vehicles, and roughly 10 hours from the 20:20 report to the 06:30 declaration of extinguishment — is consistent with the difficulty of suppressing an energized lithium-ion fire; responders relied on carbon-dioxide gaseous suppression and deliberately minimized water to avoid damaging national data, a choice that further slowed extinguishment. Crucially, the outage's breadth was set by facility policy rather than flame spread: the remaining systems were not physically damaged but were taken offline as a precautionary safety shutdown of the co-located estate, so the operational blast radius (647 systems, 709 services) reflects co-location plus shutdown policy, not an engineered dependency cascade. On the data plane, the G-Drive repository (up to 30 ministries, ~191,000 employees with access) was rendered permanently unrecoverable because it was not backed up externally, implying no isolated, restorable backup or off-site replica existed for that store. Recovery was executed as a controlled cold-start: cooling infrastructure restored first (a prerequisite for safe server operation), then sequential server restart with essential services (postal banking, delivery) prioritized and Grade-1 services tracked to a measurable 70.5 percent at Oct 24 and >95 percent thereafter. Engineering specifics that would refine this analysis — exact cell chemistry (LFP vs NMC), pack format, state-of-charge at disconnection, detection type, NFPA 855 / UL 9540A applicability, and whether the pack reignited — are not disclosed in reachable primary sources and are not asserted here; they represent standard inference points, not incident-specific findings, and do not alter the confirmed root cause.

title: NIRS Daejeon Government Data Center: UPS Lithium-Ion Battery Fire During Relocation Work
text: Failure mechanism: thermal runaway during battery relocation: The incident originated not in steady-state operation but in maintenance activity. A lithium-ion UPS battery was disconnected to be relocated to the basement, and during or after that handling it entered thermal runaway and exploded inside a server room. Two independent primary reports converge on this mechanism — the disconnected UPS lithium-ion battery as ignition source, and the explosion of lithium-ion batteries in a server room as the cited main cause. The energetic, self-sustaining nature of lithium-ion thermal runaway meant a single pack could ignite a fire that ultimately required 101 firefighters, 31 vehicles, and roughly ten hours to extinguish.

text: Why the outage reached 647 systems: The physical fire was localized, yet its operational impact was national through two distinct paths. Second, when the fire broke out all 647 co-located systems at the Daejeon headquarters were taken offline simultaneously as a preemptive safety measure, not because untouched rooms were technically dependent on the burned ones. The combined result was 647 systems offline and 709 services disrupted, sweeping in digital IDs, Korea Post postal banking and delivery, emergency GPS tracking, courts and tax — an operational blast radius set by the concentration of systems in one facility and the precautionary shutdown, well beyond the physical fire footprint.

The G-Drive cloud held work files for up to 30 ministries and had been allotted to nearly 191,000 employees (of 750,000 public-sector officials nationwide) as of August 2025. Officials confirmed the system was not backed up externally, so all documents on the repository were lost with no way to recover them, making this a permanent loss rather than an outage. title: NorthC Almere Data Center Fire: A Compartment Blaze That Took Out the Facility Power Plant and Rippled Across Dutch Public Services
text: On 7 May 2026 (around 08:45 local time) a fire broke out in a rear technical compartment of NorthC's Almere data center (Rondebeltweg) that houses power infrastructure. No servers or data carriers caught fire, but the blaze burned part of the facility's power supply and the site lost power entirely — the compute survived, yet everything went dark, and NorthC ultimately had to rebuild the power plant with new transformers and UPS. (Published reporting says only that 'part of the power supply burnt down'; that BOTH the normal and standby feeds were lost is an engineering inference from the total, multi-day power loss and the full rebuild, not an official finding.) Because multiple Dutch organizations host critical systems there, the outage cascaded outward: Utrecht University, Statistics Netherlands (CBS), public-transport operator Transdev, a regional water board, research-ICT provider Surf, IBM Cloud's Amsterdam 03, and numerous GP practices all lost service. The fire was scaled down to GRIP 1 at 20:50 that evening and to GRIP 0 with the building partially released to NorthC teams at 00:35 on 8 May, kicking off a phased restoration estimated at up to 72 hours. Temporary redundant power and cooling were activated on 13 May, roughly a week after the fire. Grid power came back building-by-building over the following weeks, with Building 1's full utility-plus-standby topology targeted for 17 July 2026. The root cause remains officially undetermined; a draft cause report was only expected at end-September 2026 because the fire-damaged structure had to be secured first.

title: NorthC Almere Data Center Fire: A Compartment Blaze That Took Out the Facility Power Plant and Rippled Across Dutch Public Services
text: Officially undetermined. As of the late-July 2026 update, NorthC had not established the cause of the fire. The on-site technical investigation could not safely begin until the fire-damaged structure was secured and water-supply work completed, so independent-expert investigation and demolition were scheduled for 27 July to 7 August 2026 and a draft cause report was pushed to end-September 2026. What is established is the failure's effect rather than its origin: a fire in a rear technical compartment burned part of the facility's power supply and produced a total facility power loss even though no servers caught fire. Published reporting states only that 'part of the power supply burnt down'; that the fire knocked out both the normal and standby feeds is inferred from the total, multi-day loss of power and the subsequent rebuild with new transformers and UPS, not from an official finding.

title: NorthC Almere Data Center Fire: A Compartment Blaze That Took Out the Facility Power Plant and Rippled Across Dutch Public Services
text: The Almere event is best understood as a power-domain failure with an intact IT domain. A fire in a rear technical compartment — the space carrying the facility's power infrastructure — burned part of the power supply and collapsed the site's usable power to zero available feeds, keeping the site dark until a temporary redundant supply was stood up on 13 May. Published reporting states only that 'part of the power supply burnt down' and that no servers or data carriers caught fire; that the event removed both the normal (utility-fed) path and the standby (generator/UPS) path is an engineering inference from the total, multi-day loss of power and the subsequent rebuild — had a standby source survived intact, the site would not have gone fully dark for days. In a correctly independent N+1 or 2N design, a single fire zone should not be able to remove both the normal and the alternate source; the recovery record suggests here it did, which is the clearest engineering signal in the public record even though the ignition cause is still undetermined. The consequence is that downstream distribution (switchgear, PDUs, rack busways) had no source to distribute, and every tenant without independent onsite generation or a live secondary site went dark despite unburned hardware. Restoration therefore had to rebuild the source layer rather than merely reboot load: temporary power and cooling were activated first (13 May) to keep the shells conditioned, then grid feeds were reintroduced building-by-building (Building 2 in the week of 25 May, Building 1 partial by end June), and finally the intended utility-plus-standby topology was to be reinstated with new transformers and UPS and generators demoted to backup, targeted for 17 July 2026. The multi-week gap between temporary power and full grid reconnection reflects long-lead electrical apparatus (transformers, UPS) and the need to re-establish the standby chain, not a software or data-recovery problem. Two engineering takeaways follow directly: fire compartmentation must guarantee that no single zone contains both the primary and backup power paths, and detection/suppression in power compartments must be sized to prevent a technical-space fire from becoming a total-source-loss event. Definitive design conclusions await NorthC's independent investigation and draft cause report expected end-September 2026, after the 27 July–7 August demolition and expert examination.

title: OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)
text: In the early hours of 10 March 2021 a fire broke out in a ground-floor energy room at OVHcloud's SBG2 facility in Strasbourg, where the site's UPS units and their lead-acid battery banks were housed. Video surveillance and the fire panel traced the initiating event to a near-simultaneous electrical fault on UPS2 and its connected batteries. With no automatic suppression system in any of the five campus buildings, and a free-cooling design that used intumescent-treated raw-wood floors and single-skin cladding to aid airflow, the fire spread through the entire structure. De-energisation was slow because there was no accessible general site cut-off, forcing the grid operator to isolate an upstream substation; current was still present in the burning building well after the cut order. SBG2 was destroyed in its entirety, four of twelve rooms in adjacent SBG1 were partially destroyed, and the SBG2–SBG3 inter-building link was impacted. Roughly 30,000 servers were lost and about 3.6 million websites went offline. There were no casualties or injuries. French investigator BEA-RI could establish the fault location but not its precise cause, leaving several hypotheses open pending a court-expert examination.

title: OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)
text: The fire originated on the ground floor of SBG2 in the energy room complex housing the UPS units and their lead-acid battery banks. Video surveillance and the site fire-control panel establish an electrical fault at UPS2 and at the batteries connected to it (the two were in separate rooms), with fire outbreaks appearing almost simultaneously on the batteries and on an inverter. The precise cause of the UPS failure could not be established by BEA-RI; candidate hypotheses include liquid or humidity from the nearby cooling system, a fault linked to a maintenance operation performed the same morning, or operation of the inverter outside its normal ranges. The ambiguity is deepened by the use of lead-acid (not lithium) batteries, which BEA-RI characterises as more robust and stable, with internal short circuits being rare. The precise ignition mechanism was left to an ongoing court-expert examination.

title: OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)
text: The initiating event sits in the UPS/battery topology of SBG2's ground-floor energy rooms. BEA-RI's forensic basis is the site's own video surveillance and fire-control panel telemetry, which localise an electrical fault to UPS2 and to the lead-acid battery string connected to it — with the UPS and its batteries deliberately sited in separate rooms. Fire outbreaks registered almost simultaneously on the batteries and on an inverter, indicating the fault propagated across the charging chain rather than being confined to a single component. SBG2's battery population was substantial: 800 lead-acid units of roughly 30 kg and 13 kW unit power each. Because lead-acid chemistry is comparatively stable and internal shorts are rare, BEA-RI could not close out the ignition cause and enumerated three non-exclusive hypotheses — ingress of liquid/humidity from the physically adjacent cooling system, a defect introduced by the maintenance operation performed the same morning, or operation of the inverter outside its qualified envelope — deferring the definitive determination to a court-expert. The decisive engineering weakness was the response envelope, not merely the fault. With detection but no automatic suppression, and no local general cut-off, the facility could not be made electrically safe fast enough to permit water: the cut order at 00:58 propagated only to the upstream SER (Strasbourg Électricité Réseaux) source substation effective at 01:50, yet 02:14 telemetry showed SBG2 still energised and fire spreading to SBG1, and full de-energisation was achieved only at 03:28. In parallel, the water side was undersized — one hydrant below 60 m3/h, no on-site reserve, and no Rhine-canal pumping means — so effective flow depended on the fireboat. The building fabric closed the loop: intumescent-treated raw-wood floors and single-skin/aluminium cladding, engineered for free-cooling heat exchange, provided combustible vertical pathways and negligible compartmentation. The net systemic failure mode is the coincidence of a low-probability power-electronics fault with an environment offering no independent means of early suppression, rapid isolation, or adequate water — the hallmark of insufficient defence-in-depth around the energy plant.

title: OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)
text: Failure mechanism: an undetermined fault in the power backbone: The incident began not in the IT halls but in SBG2's power backbone. Surveillance and the fire panel place the initiating electrical fault on UPS2 and its associated lead-acid battery bank, with outbreaks appearing almost simultaneously on batteries and an inverter located in a separate room. Crucially, BEA-RI could not establish why the UPS failed, floating three hypotheses — liquid or humidity from the adjacent cooling system, a fault tied to a maintenance operation performed that same morning, or operation of the inverter outside normal ranges. The use of lead-acid rather than lithium chemistry, which BEA-RI regards as robust and rarely subject to internal short circuits, makes the ignition all the more anomalous and is why the precise mechanism was handed to a court-appointed expert.

title: OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)
text: Why it cascaded: a design optimised against containment: Several deliberate design choices converted a localised electrical fault into a total loss. No automatic suppression existed in any of the five buildings, so water could not be applied until power was cut. The free-cooling architecture — intumescent-treated raw-wood floors and single-skin/aluminium cladding chosen to maximise heat exchange and minimise cooling energy — offered combustible pathways and little compartmentation, and responders judged on arrival that it would not permit containment. Compounding this, there was no accessible general cut-off: de-energisation had to wait for an upstream substation isolation, and current was still present in the fully-ablaze building at 02:14, more than an hour after the 00:58 cut order. Each efficiency- or cost-driven decision individually plausible combined into a system with no early line of defence.

title: OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)
text: Recovery: external water, mass replacement, and cross-site failover: With one hydrant under 60 m3/h and no on-site reserve or canal-pumping capability, effective firefighting depended on the EUROPA fireboat, which arrived around 02:57, and on full de-energisation at 03:28; the fire was controlled by 06:45 and extinguished by 10:02, with the intervention closed at 18:13 and no casualties. Service recovery leaned on the surviving campus and OVH's manufacturing: SBG3 and SBG4 restarted from 17 March, the Croix factory doubled output from 1,500 to over 3,000 servers per week, and by 23 April Bare Metal, Public Cloud and VPS were roughly 98–99% re-delivered while Hosted Private Cloud reached 88% on other sites, with 8,000 services slated to return on their original IPs. Customers who suffered permanent data loss, however, could not be made whole by capacity alone.

title: OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)
text: Organisational and systemic factors: The investigation frames the loss less as a freak accident than as an accumulation of risk-acceptance decisions: choosing no suppression across the whole campus, building for cooling efficiency over fire compartmentation, and not meeting the initial ICPE water-resource requirements. BEA-RI's remedies are structural — redefine the regulated 'charging workshop' to cover batteries plus charging equipment, drill electrical-securing procedures, audit the entire fleet for fire vulnerability, and monitor battery state proactively. Notably, BEA-RI concluded data centers should not be ICPE-classified, arguing the dominant consequence of such a fire is economic and strategic (data loss and service unavailability) rather than human or environmental, and pointing instead to professional fire-safety guides and ANSSI certification.

title: OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)
text: Cross-incident pattern: single-facility concentration and thin defence-in-depth: SBG2 is a canonical example of correlated failure: tens of thousands of servers and millions of dependent websites concentrated in one building whose defensive layers — suppression, compartmentation, rapid de-energisation, and water supply — were all thin or absent simultaneously, so a single power-room fault removed everything at once. The recurring lesson mirrors other large outages: efficiency and cost optimisations that quietly erode independent safety layers, plus customer over-reliance on a single site without geo-redundant backups, turn a contained component fault into a headline loss. Resilience here was ultimately proven not by the facility's own defences but by cross-site failover and industrial replacement capacity.

title: Red Sea Subsea Cable Cuts — Rubymar Anchor Severs AAE-1, Seacom/TGN-EA and EIG off Yemen
text: On 24 February 2024 three submarine cable systems — Seacom (which Kentik groups with TGN-EA), AAE-1 and EIG — were severed off the west coast of Yemen in the Red Sea. The generally-accepted cause is the anchor of the MV Rubymar, an abandoned cargo ship struck by Houthi forces on 18 February, dragging across the cable corridor after the anchor was dropped when the vessel came under fire. The cuts degraded a large share of Asia-Europe-Middle-East transit (commonly cited at ~25%, though that figure is unattributed in reachable sources) and were felt across East Africa and the Middle East. Physical repair did not begin until July 2024, when an E-Marine cable ship restored AAE-1 first and then the remaining two cables. The cause is the accepted narrative rather than a forensic consortium finding; TGN-EA is named alongside Seacom by Kentik, but whether it is a physically distinct 4th cable or shares the Seacom system remains only partly corroborated.

title: Red Sea Subsea Cable Cuts — Rubymar Anchor Severs AAE-1, Seacom/TGN-EA and EIG off Yemen
text: The generally-accepted cause is that the MV Rubymar — an abandoned cargo ship struck by Houthi forces on 18 February 2024 — dropped its anchor when fired upon, and the drifting/dragging anchor damaged the submarine cables in proximity (Seacom/TGN-EA, AAE-1 and EIG) off the west coast of Yemen. This is explicitly the consensus account ('It's generally accepted'; Kentik frames it as the 'leading theory'), NOT a forensic finding: no cable consortium published a joint root-cause report, and the physical geometry by which a single vessel's anchor severed multiple distinct cable systems, the exact cut coordinates, and landing points remain unproven in reachable sources.

title: Red Sea Subsea Cable Cuts — Rubymar Anchor Severs AAE-1, Seacom/TGN-EA and EIG off Yemen
text: The fault signature is consistent with a moving-anchor bottom contact rather than a static single-point break. Submarine cables in the Bab-el-Mandeb approach lie within a constrained corridor across the shallow continental margin off Yemen's west coast, where anchor-drag is the dominant physical threat. A vessel adrift with its anchor deployed does not sever a cable cleanly at one coordinate; it plows a track along the seabed, so contacting several separate systems (Seacom/TGN-EA, AAE-1, EIG) in a single drift is geometrically plausible if those cables cross the drift path — but the exact coordinates, the drift vector, and the cable-crossing geometry were never published, so the multi-cable severance remains an accepted inference rather than a reconstructed fact. The failure timing was inferred externally from BGP: as each cable's capacity dropped, dependent prefixes withdrew and re-advertised over surviving paths, producing discrete reconvergence clusters (Doug Madory / Kentik place the Seacom failure, marked by loss of Tata/TGN transit, near 09:46 UTC and AAE-1 near 09:51 UTC). That ~5-minute spacing is itself evidence of a moving hazard touching cables sequentially, though it is analyst-derived, not operator-timestamped. On restoration: subsea repair requires a cable ship to grapple the fault, cut out the damaged section, splice in a new length with a repeater-compatible joint, and re-lay the bight — a per-fault operation of days under normal conditions. Here the binding constraint was not splice time but access: the ~5-month gap to July 2024 reflects the security/permit barrier of operating a cable ship in an active conflict zone. Once on site, a single E-Marine (e&) vessel amortized that access cost by repairing AAE-1 first and then staying to complete Seacom and EIG, which is why the three restorations fall in one July window despite unpublished individual completion dates.

title: Red Sea Subsea Cable Cuts — Rubymar Anchor Severs AAE-1, Seacom/TGN-EA and EIG off Yemen
text: Failure mechanism: The event is a classic anchor-drag cable fault, but with a conflict twist. The MV Rubymar was struck by Houthi forces on 18 February 2024 and abandoned; left adrift with its anchor down, that anchor dragged across the seabed in the Bab-el-Mandeb cable corridor off Yemen's west coast and contacted three submarine systems — Seacom (which Kentik groups with TGN-EA), AAE-1 and EIG. Crucially, this is the 'generally accepted' / 'leading theory' account rather than a forensically established one: no consortium published cut coordinates or a mechanical reconstruction of how one anchor severed multiple distinct cables, so the mechanism, while plausible and widely accepted, is not proven at RCA rigor.

title: Red Sea Subsea Cable Cuts — Rubymar Anchor Severs AAE-1, Seacom/TGN-EA and EIG off Yemen
text: Why it cascaded: The cascade was geographic, not logical. Multiple independent Asia-Europe backbones share the narrow Red Sea chokepoint, so a single dragging anchor could sever several systems in one pass — eliminating the redundancy those separate cables were meant to provide. BGP telemetry captured the failures as tightly-spaced clusters (analyst attribution places the Seacom failure, including loss of Tata/TGN transit, near 09:46 UTC and AAE-1 near 09:51 UTC), consistent with one moving object contacting cables in sequence. The result was degradation of a large share of Asia-Europe/Middle-East transit, commonly cited at ~25% though that figure is unattributed in reachable sources.

title: Red Sea Subsea Cable Cuts — Rubymar Anchor Severs AAE-1, Seacom/TGN-EA and EIG off Yemen
text: Recovery: Recovery was defined by delay. The cut occurred on 24 February 2024, but physical repair did not begin until July 2024 — roughly five months — because the conflict environment constrained cable-ship access. When repair did proceed, a single E-Marine vessel (a subsidiary of Emirates Telecommunications Group / e&) restored AAE-1 first, then remained on station to repair the other two, Seacom and EIG. Traffic ran on rerouted capacity throughout the interim. Exact per-cable completion dates were never individually published, leaving the restoration timeline coarse.

First, information opacity: the only hard financial figure came not from an operator but from a downstream shareholder — Remgro disclosed that Seacom's contribution to its headline earnings fell from ~R32M to ~R2M, attributed to once-off repair costs, yet the absolute repair spend and any affected-user count were never disclosed. Second, attribution weakness: the widely-repeated ~25% traffic and 'tens of millions of users' figures trace to no named organization in the dossier's reachable sources, so the incident's true magnitude cannot be independently verified. The absence of a joint consortium root-cause report compounds both problems.

It also echoes the broader difficulty of attributing subsea faults — 'accident' versus deliberate action, and 'accepted' versus forensically proven — a recurring ambiguity in Red Sea and Baltic cable events alike.

title: Google Cloud Accidentally Deletes UniSuper's Entire GCVE Private Cloud
text: During the initial provisioning of UniSuper's Google Cloud VMware Engine (GCVE) Private Cloud, one input parameter was left blank in an internal Google deployment tool. Per Google's disclosure the blank value caused the system to assign a then-unknown default fixed one-year term to the Private Cloud, which silently armed an automatic-deletion action. Roughly a year later, at the end of that system-assigned term, the Private Cloud was deleted across both of its copies. The A$135B fund's 647,000+ members lost access to online services for nine days. The deletion did not reach data backups stored in Google Cloud Storage in the same region, which — together with third-party backup software — enabled a rebuild rather than permanent data loss. Members' account balances and investments were not lost, and the incident was operational, not a cyberattack.

title: Google Cloud Accidentally Deletes UniSuper's Entire GCVE Private Cloud
text: Operator/tooling misconfiguration via a defaulted term value. Per Google, the system assigned a then-unknown default fixed one-year term for that parameter, and at the end of the system-assigned year the Private Cloud was automatically deleted. Google's blog phrases the blank passively while Miles Ward's later account attributes the null to a creation-script bug — either way it was an inadvertent misconfiguration, NOT a customer action, a cyberattack, or a data-integrity/hardware fault.

title: Google Cloud Accidentally Deletes UniSuper's Entire GCVE Private Cloud
text: The chain, per Google's disclosure, is precise and closes on the parameter's semantics even though Google never names the field itself. During initial GCVE Private Cloud provisioning through an internal tool, one input parameter was left blank. Rather than validating for a required value, the system assigned a then-unknown default: a fixed one-year term for that parameter. This is the load-bearing detail — the blank did not merely leave a setting empty; it bound the Private Cloud to a lifecycle attribute (term/expiry) that carried an automatic-deletion action at term end. The value sat latent and unmonitored for the full period. After the end of the system-assigned one-year term, the platform's lifecycle machinery executed the deletion of the Private Cloud. Because the deletion targeted the subscription-level logical resource, it removed both replicated copies simultaneously — redundancy at the data/copy layer offers no protection against an authoritative delete of the resource above it. The single surviving fault-boundary was storage scope: data backups in Google Cloud Storage in the same region were outside the deletion's target set and were untouched, and third-party backup software provided the tooling to reconstitute state. Recovery was therefore a full rebuild-from-backup rather than a failover: teams restored network and security configurations, then applications, then data, over several days of 24x7 work, yielding a nine-day member-facing blackout. Several residual technical unknowns remain in the public record: Google does not name the specific input field; sources diverge on whether the blank was a manual operator omission or a creation-script bug that passed a null value (Miles Ward's 21 May account suggests the latter); sources also describe the two deleted copies inconsistently as 'two geographies' (8 May joint statement) versus 'two zones' (Google's technical write-up and itnews); and Google does not state whether the internal-tool 'fixed term' path shares the same soft-delete/expireTime mechanism exposed by the public GCVE API, so it is unconfirmed whether a standard soft-delete grace window existed on this internal deletion path. The absence of any effective cool-off, approval gate, or expiry-visibility surface is the key engineering gap: a destructive, delayed action executed with neither a warning nor a reversible-hold window in front of it.

text: Failure mechanism: a blank field became a one-year self-destruct: The proximate cause was mundane: while standing up UniSuper's GCVE Private Cloud through an internal deployment tool, a single input parameter was left blank. title: Google Cloud Accidentally Deletes UniSuper's Entire GCVE Private Cloud
text: Why it hit both copies: UniSuper's Private Cloud was replicated across two copies — described as 'two geographies' in the joint statement and 'two zones' in Google's technical detail — an architecture intended to survive the loss of a single copy. A control-plane 'delete this Private Cloud' action targets the logical resource, so both copies were removed together. This is the classic distinction between fault-tolerance and blast-radius containment: redundancy multiplies copies of the data but does not multiply protection against an authoritative command to destroy the resource. The single armed timer was, in effect, a correlated-failure source sitting above the redundancy layer, which is precisely why the outcome was total rather than degraded.

title: Google Cloud Accidentally Deletes UniSuper's Entire GCVE Private Cloud

title: Google Cloud Accidentally Deletes UniSuper's Entire GCVE Private Cloud
text: Cross-incident pattern: unsafe defaults and destructive automation: This event sits in a well-worn category of cloud and infrastructure failures where a routine operational input, mishandled by automation, produces disproportionate destruction.
